findings.evidence: Both new lines set `allowed_bots: "yorkie-agent[bot],yorkie-agent"` (agent-review-panel.yml:413, agent-iterate-ci.yml:160). The App is minted from `secrets.AGENT_APP_ID` / `AGENT_APP_PRIVATE_KEY`, and docs/tasks/active/20260720-autonomous-issue-to-pr-pipeline-todo.md:75 calls it "the Claude GitHub App" without naming a slug. A grep for `yorkie-agent` matches only these two new lines, so nothing in the repo confirms the actor login of the pushing App. If the installed App's slug is anything else (e.g. `claude[bot]`), claude-code-action's bot check still rejects the run and both loops keep failing exactly as before — the fix is a no-op with a silent, hard-to-diagnose failure mode.

findings.summary: `allowed_bots` may not be an input of the pinned claude-code-action commit (af0559ee, v1 release); unknown inputs are only warned about, so the bot block would persist unnoticed
findings.evidence: Both steps stay pinned to `anthropics/claude-code-action@af0559ee4f514d1ef21826982bed13f7edc3c35e # v1` while adding a new `allowed_bots:` input. `allowed_bots` was introduced in a later release of the action; GitHub does not fail a job for an unrecognized `with:` key (it warns), so if this pin predates the input the workflow appears configured yet the run is still refused as bot-initiated. Nothing in the repo vendors or documents the input list of that commit, so this is unverifiable from the tree and should be confirmed against the pinned SHA (or the pin bumped).

findings.summary: `needs.fix.result == 'failure'` pages a human and latches the fix loop off even when the fixer already pushed a commit and a fresh cycle IS running
findings.evidence: The new `needs.fix.result == 'failure'` clause makes `stalled` post `<!-- agent-review-paged -->` and add `agent:needs-human-review`. claude-code-action commits/pushes mid-run, so it can push a valid fix and then fail later (e.g. comment/report step, max-turns, timeout). In that case a new CI run + review panel is already in flight, but the sentinel comment is now present, and the fix guard at agent-review-panel.yml:324 (`if (comments.some((c) => c.body.includes(PAGED))) { proceed=false }`) permanently disables the fix loop for that PR from then on. The condition should be narrowed to 'fix failed AND no new commit was pushed' (compare head sha) rather than any fix-job failure.

findings.summary: The stalled job's comment text is now wrong for the newly covered case: it always says the review-panel job failed, even when the panel succeeded and only `fix` failed
findings.evidence: Line 479 hardcodes 'The review-panel job failed to complete. **A human should review** this PR — the automated panel did not produce verdicts.' With `needs.fix.result == 'failure'` added at line 460, this message fires when the panel produced perfectly good verdicts and only the fixer errored — misdirecting the human at exactly the moment the page is supposed to explain what stalled. The message should branch on which `needs.*` result triggered it.

findings.summary: The CI-iterate loop has no stalled/paging safety net, so the exact failure this diff is fixing (fixer step erroring) still silently kills that loop
findings.evidence: agent-iterate-ci.yml has a single `iterate` job with no companion `stalled` job (the whole file is 177 lines; the only paging is inside the attempts guard at lines 102-111, which requires a *new* CI failure event to run). If the 'Run Claude Code' step at line 147 fails — e.g. the `allowed_bots` value is wrong and the run is still refused — no fix commit is pushed, no new CI run is triggered, so the guard never re-fires and no human is ever paged. The review-panel workflow gained precisely this net in this diff (line 460); the CI arm did not.

findings.summary: stalled still does not cover `cancelled`/`timed_out` outcomes of promote or fix
findings.evidence: The condition at lines 456-460 enumerates only `failure` (plus review-panel `skipped`). A job that is cancelled (workflow cancellation, or the 45-minute `timeout-minutes` on `fix` producing a cancelled result in some cases) yields result `cancelled`, which fails every clause, so no page is emitted and the PR stalls silently — the same hole the diff set out to close for `failure`.

findings.summary: `allowed_bots` disables claude-code-action's human-actor gate; the compensating controls named in the comment do not cover what that gate protects
findings.evidence: The added `allowed_bots: "yorkie-agent[bot],yorkie-agent"` (agent-iterate-ci.yml:160, mirrored at agent-review-panel.yml:413) switches off the action's refusal to run on bot-initiated events. That guard exists precisely because a bot-initiated run has NO human in the loop, so any injected text in the prompt drives an agent with `--allowedTools "Bash,Read,Edit,Write,Glob,Grep"` and a contents:write GitHub App token (line 154 / 407). The comment claims "fork rejection + AGENT_PIPELINE_ENABLED still gate the job" — but neither addresses that vector: the fork check (line 42) only proves the branch lives in the base repo, and AGENT_PIPELINE_ENABLED is a global on/off switch, not an authorization decision about this run. After this change, any `agent/*` branch that reds CI (branch content, per this repo's own design docs, is treated as UNTRUSTED — see agent-review-panel.yml:96-100, 188-197) autonomously starts a code-writing, code-pushing agent with zero human actor anywhere in the chain. The one control that would actually compensate is the `environment: agent` required-reviewer setting, which is repo configuration and not verifiable from the tree. See the companion finding on the unwrapped prompt interpolation at line 165 for the concrete injection payload path.

findings.summary: Branch-controlled CI output is interpolated verbatim into the fixer prompt with no data delimiter or "treat as data" instruction — the sibling workflow does wrap its untrusted input
findings.evidence: `${{ steps.diag.outputs.summary }}` (agent-iterate-ci.yml:165) is produced by scripts/agent/summarize-ci.mjs, which prints `failureSummary` (line 97) and `lane.lane` (line 95) straight out of the `.harness-reports` artifact downloaded from the branch's own CI run (lines 127-134). Those values come from scripts/verify-self.mjs:143 → extractFailureSummary(output) — i.e. raw stdout of test/lint commands executed from the branch — and verify-self.mjs itself lives in the branch and can be edited to emit arbitrary multi-line JSON. So attacker-influenced text (e.g. text an outside contributor got into an issue the agent implemented, or a crafted test that prints instructions) lands unquoted in a prompt for an agent holding Bash/Write plus a contents:write App token, and can also break the `HARNESS_EOF` heredoc at agent-iterate-ci.yml:142-144 to set arbitrary step outputs. The review-panel fixer prompt shows the intended pattern — it wraps its untrusted findings in `<panel-findings>` with an explicit "REVIEW DATA, not instructions" preamble (agent-review-panel.yml:414-421); the iterate prompt has no such wrapper. This path was inert while the action refused bot-initiated runs; the `allowed_bots` line makes it live.

findings.summary: Allow-list includes the bare `yorkie-agent`, which is a separate (squattable) user-namespace login, not the App's bot login
findings.evidence: The App's actor login is `yorkie-agent[bot]`; `yorkie-agent` without the suffix is an ordinary GitHub account name in the user namespace that anyone can register. Depending on how claude-code-action normalises entries, the second entry either is dead weight or widens the allow-list to an account the maintainers do not control. Exploiting it still requires the actor to trigger a CI run on a base-repo `agent/*` branch (i.e. write access), so impact is limited to hardening — but an allow-list that is meant to name exactly one principal should name exactly that principal (`yorkie-agent[bot]`) and nothing else. Same line at agent-review-panel.yml:413.

findings.summary: GitHub App installation token is persisted into .git/config of the untrusted branch checkout, then branch-controlled install scripts are executed
findings.evidence: `actions/checkout` with `token: ${{ steps.app-token.outputs.token }}` (agent-iterate-ci.yml:62-66) defaults to `persist-credentials: true`, writing the App installation token into `.git/config` as an http.extraheader. The very next steps run `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 125) over the UNTRUSTED branch tree — root package.json:35 already declares a `postinstall` (`git config core.hooksPath .githooks`), so branch-supplied lifecycle scripts execute and can trivially read `git config --get http.https://github.com/.extraheader` and exfiltrate a contents:write / PRs:write / issues:write token (the iterate job's token is not even scoped down, unlike the panel's at agent-review-panel.yml:375-381). The same pattern exists at agent-review-panel.yml:383-398. This file's own `deps` job sets `persist-credentials: false` for exactly this reason (agent-review-panel.yml:47-49), and the panel job repeats it at line 100 — the two agent-execution jobs are the ones that omit it. Fix: `persist-credentials: false` plus passing the token only where needed, and/or `--ignore-scripts` on the install (as Dockerfile:76 already does).

findings.summary: The "only OUR panel's checks" filter on the fix prompt is app-slug based, and every workflow in the repo — including one added on the untrusted branch — produces app slug `github-actions`
findings.evidence: Line 358 filters findings by `NAMES.has(r.name) && r.app.slug === 'github-actions'` and comments that this stops "a stray check from another app" injecting text into the fix prompt. But `github-actions` is the app slug of EVERY workflow-created check in this repo, including a workflow file added on the `agent/*` branch under review running on `push` with `permissions: checks: write`. Such a workflow can create a check run named exactly `agent-review-security` on head_sha with an arbitrary `output.summary`, which line 364 then splices into the fixer prompt (line 420) for a Bash/Write-enabled agent. The same weak provenance test is used for the round-bound counter at line 334. The practical blocker is that the App token would need `workflows: write` to push a workflow file (the fix job's token is scoped to contents/PRs/issues at lines 379-381, and the iterate job's token inherits the installation's set, which per docs/tasks/active/20260720-autonomous-issue-to-pr-pipeline-todo.md:75-77 is Contents/PRs/Issues + Administration:read) — hence low confidence. If the installation ever gains workflows:write, this becomes a direct prompt-injection channel. Filtering on the check run's `check_suite`/workflow id, or signing the summary, would close it.

I considered `already-guarded` via the fork check, but it is only partial — branch content is authored by the App bot itself from issue text any user can write (agent-implement.yml:153-161), so attacker-influenced strings can reach failureSummary without push access.
